texts.title: Working from anywhere
texts.text: Three years ago, Anna's company announced that employees could work from anywhere. At first she was thrilled: no commute, flexible hours and the freedom to travel. She spent one winter in Portugal and the next spring in Georgia, working from cafés and rented flats. However, the reality turned out to be more complicated than the photos on social media. Unstable internet connections made video calls frustrating, and time differences meant she sometimes had to join meetings at midnight. Even worse, she realized she had stopped talking to her colleagues about anything except work. "I'd been so focused on the freedom that I hadn't noticed how isolated I'd become," she admits. Nowadays Anna has found a compromise. She rents a desk in a coworking space, visits the office once a month and sets strict limits on her working hours. "Remote work isn't a dream or a nightmare," she says. "It's a tool. Whether it works depends on how you use it."

questions.q: What was the biggest unexpected problem for Anna?
Why did she sometimes join meetings at midnight?
options: Because she preferred working at night
Because her internet was faster then

questions.q: What is Anna's opinion of remote work now?
options: It's a tool that depends on how you use it

texts.title: The return of wooden skyscrapers
texts.text: For more than a century, tall buildings have been made of steel and reinforced concrete. Recently, however, engineers have been rediscovering a much older material: wood. Modern "mass timber" consists of thin layers of wood glued together under pressure, which makes the panels surprisingly strong. Supporters claim that it is more sustainable than concrete, because trees absorb carbon dioxide while they grow, whereas producing cement releases huge amounts of it. Wooden panels are also lighter, so the foundation can be smaller, and they are made in factories, which means construction sites are quieter and projects finish faster. Critics, on the other hand, point to the risk of fire. Supporters reply that thick timber burns slowly and forms a protective black layer on the outside, so the load-bearing structure remains stable for a long time. Building regulations in many countries have already been changed to allow wooden towers of up to eighteen floors. If the trend continues, the skyline of the future might look surprisingly natural.

questions.q: Why do supporters say wood is more sustainable?
What is the main concern of critics?
Why can the foundation be smaller?

texts.title: Is esports a real career?
texts.text: When Daniel told his parents that he wanted to become a professional gamer, they assumed it was a phase. He was sixteen, and he had been playing a team shooter for eight hours a day. Two years later, he signed his first contract with an esports organization. The reality of professional gaming, he explains, has little to do with having fun. Players follow a strict routine: tactics meetings in the morning, scrimmages against other teams in the afternoon and video analysis of their mistakes in the evening. Many teams now employ coaches, psychologists and even nutrition experts, because physical and mental health have a significant impact on performance. Careers are short, though. Reaction time tends to decline in a player's mid-twenties, and only a small percentage of players earn enough to live on. That is why Daniel is studying computer science online. "Esports taught me discipline and teamwork," he says. "But I'd be naive to rely only on it. I want a plan B."

questions.q: How did Daniel's parents react at first?
options: They bought him a new PC

questions.q: Why do teams employ psychologists and nutrition experts?
Why is Daniel studying computer science?
options: Esports careers are short and risky

texts.title: Four stages of culture shock
texts.text: Psychologists often describe culture shock in four stages. The first is the "honeymoon": everything in the new country seems exciting, from the food to the architecture. After a few weeks or months comes frustration. Simple tasks, such as opening a bank account or understanding a joke, suddenly feel exhausting, and many people feel homesick. Some even consider going back. The third stage is adjustment. You start to recognize patterns, you make a few local friends and the language stops being a wall. Finally comes adaptation: you feel comfortable in both cultures, even though you will probably never lose your accent. Experts emphasize that these stages are not the same for everyone, and people can move back and forth between them. Their advice is surprisingly practical: learn the language before you move rather than after, keep a routine, join clubs or sports teams, and don't compare your first year abroad with your whole life at home. As one expat put it, "It gets easier — not because the country changes, but because you do."

questions.q: What happens in the second stage?
options: People feel comfortable in both cultures

questions.q: When do experts suggest learning the language?
options: Only if you plan to stay

questions.q: According to the expat, why does it get easier?
